+def _record_json(record, location_text):
+    """_encode_json(record) for a _record_estimate record whose backtrace is
+    still empty, reusing location_text, the encoded location it was updated
+    with. Falls back to _encode_json for unexpected value types."""
+    sequence = record["sequence"]
+    elapsed = record["elapsed_ms"]
+    thread_id = record["thread_id"]
+    index = record["breakpoint_index"]
+    receiver_class = record["receiver_class"]
+    selector = record["selector"]
+    if (
+        type(sequence) is not int
+        or type(thread_id) is not int
+        or type(index) is not int
+        or type(elapsed) not in (int, float)
+        or elapsed - elapsed != 0
+        or not (receiver_class is None or type(receiver_class) is str)
+        or not (selector is None or type(selector) is str)
+        or len(location_text) < 3
+    ):
+        return _encode_json(record)
+    parts = []
+    for register in record["registers"]:
+        name = register["name"]
+        value = register["value"]
+        if type(name) is not str or type(value) is not str:
+            return _encode_json(record)
+        parts.append(
+            '{"name": %s, "value": %s}'
+            % (_encode_json_string(name), _encode_json_string(value))
+        )
+    return (
+        '{"sequence": %s, "elapsed_ms": %s, "thread_id": %s, '
+        '"breakpoint_index": %s, "receiver_class": %s, "selector": %s, '
+        '"registers": [%s], "backtrace": [], %s'
+        % (
+            int.__repr__(sequence),
+            type(elapsed).__repr__(elapsed),
+            int.__repr__(thread_id),
+            int.__repr__(index),
+            "null" if receiver_class is None else _encode_json_string(receiver_class),
+            "null" if selector is None else _encode_json_string(selector),
+            ", ".join(parts),
+            location_text[1:],
+        )
+    )

actions.reason: On every breakpoint hit, _handle_breakpoint ran _encode_json over the whole record. That included the five location keys, even though the encoded location text is already cached in the _frame_location entry for later backtrace use. A new helper, _record_json, builds the same JSON text directly. Integers and floats are written with their repr, strings with json's encode_basestring_ascii, and register dicts in a fixed key order. The cached location text (entry[2], encoded on first use) is appended after the empty backtrace. If any value has an unexpected type, or the float is not finite, the helper falls back to _encode_json. Output is byte-identical to json.dumps defaults. Measured hits_ir ratio 0.9296, with identical equivalence outputs.

journal.text:
I read _handle_breakpoint in bridge/native/rea_lldb_tracer.py. On every breakpoint hit it called _encode_json on the whole record. That record includes the five location keys, whose encoded text is already cached in the _frame_location entry. I added a helper, _record_json, that builds the same JSON text directly. It writes integers and floats with repr, strings with json's encode_basestring_ascii, and reuses the cached location text. I made small edits at two call sites near lines 614 and 650.

In the sandbox, hits_ir went from 573088593 to 532721171, a ratio of 0.9296. report_ir went from 484614811 to 486472508, a ratio of 1.0038, so the report path got slightly worse. Outputs were identical, both builds passed, and the guard was ok with 58 lines in 1 file. The candidate is submitted and queued for independent replay.

I now believe generic JSON encoding is a real cost per hit in this tracer, and cached fragments are worth reusing.

Next I would look at why report_ir rose and check whether other per-hit encoders can reuse cached text.
